questions.question: What grievance drives the citizens' unrest at the opening?

options.text: Hunger and the belief that the powerful are withholding corn.
A demand that Rome abandon every war against the Volscians.
The loss of the city's temples to Aufidius's soldiers.
A law requiring every citizen to leave Rome that day.

questions.explanation: The citizens contrast their hunger with patrician abundance and demand corn at an affordable price.

evidence.exact:
FIRST CITIZEN.
We are accounted poor citizens, the patricians good. What authority surfeits on would relieve us. If they would yield us but the superfluity while it were wholesome, we might guess they relieved us humanely. But they think we are too dear. The leanness that afflicts us, the object of our misery, is as an inventory to particularize their abundance; our sufferance is a gain to them. Let us revenge this with our pikes ere we become rakes; for the gods know I speak this in hunger for bread, not in thirst for revenge.

questions.question: What point does Menenius make with his fable of the belly and the body's members?

options.text: The city's hunger proves that Rome has no useful leaders.
The Senate serves the whole city by distributing benefits.
The citizens must replace the Senate with foreign rulers.
Soldiers should refuse food until the tribunes surrender.

questions.explanation: Menenius identifies the Senate with the belly and argues that its work nourishes the rest of the state.

evidence.exact:
MENENIUS.
The senators of Rome are this good belly,
And you the mutinous members. For examine
Their counsels and their cares, digest things rightly
Touching the weal o’ th’ common, you shall find
No public benefit which you receive
But it proceeds or comes from them to you
And no way from yourselves. What do you think,
You, the great toe of this assembly?
evidence.prefix: an answer. How apply you this?
evidence.suffix:

I the great toe

questions.question: Why is Caius Martius given the name Coriolanus?

options.text: To celebrate his marriage into Aufidius's family.
To reward his decision to distribute free corn.
To honor his deeds in the fighting at Corioles.
To mark his appointment as Rome's sole tribune.

questions.explanation: Cominius grants the added name in recognition of Martius's service at Corioles.

evidence.exact:
COMINIUS.
Too modest are you,
More cruel to your good report than grateful
To us that give you truly. By your patience,
If ’gainst yourself you be incensed, we’ll put you,
Like one that means his proper harm, in manacles,
Then reason safely with you. Therefore be it known,
As to us to all the world, that Caius Martius
Wears this war’s garland, in token of the which
My noble steed, known to the camp, I give him,
With all his trim belonging. And from this time,
For what he did before Corioles, call him,
With all th’ applause and clamour of the host,
Caius Martius Coriolanus! Bear
Th’ addition nobly ever!
evidence.prefix:
d
In praises sauced with lies.

questions.question: How do Sicinius and Brutus turn the citizens against Coriolanus's election?

options.text: They stress his contempt and urge the citizens to revoke their votes.
They announce that he has already accepted the Volscian crown.
They reveal that he has never served in the Roman army.
They promise to crown Volumnia if the citizens support her son.

questions.explanation: The tribunes argue that his pride threatens the people's liberties and tell them to undo their election.

evidence.exact:
SICINIUS.
Let them assemble
And, on a safer judgment, all revoke
Your ignorant election. Enforce his pride
And his old hate unto you. Besides, forget not
With what contempt he wore the humble weed,
How in his suit he scorned you; but your loves,
Thinking upon his services, took from you
Th’ apprehension of his present portance,
Which most gibingly, ungravely, he did fashion
After the inveterate hate he bears you.

questions.question: How does Coriolanus answer Rome when he is sentenced to banishment?

options.text: He asks Menenius to take the blame and leave in his place.
He declares that he banishes the citizens and turns his back on the city.
He begs the tribunes to let him remain as their servant.
He agrees to retire quietly and never bear arms again.

questions.explanation: Coriolanus answers exile with contempt, declaring that there is a world elsewhere.

evidence.exact:
CORIOLANUS.
You common cry of curs, whose breath I hate
As reek o’ th’ rotten fens, whose loves I prize
As the dead carcasses of unburied men
That do corrupt my air, I banish you!
And here remain with your uncertainty;
Let every feeble rumour shake your hearts;
Your enemies, with nodding of their plumes,
Fan you into despair! Have the power still
To banish your defenders, till at length
Your ignorance—which finds not till it feels,
Making but reservation of yourselves,
Still your own foes—deliver you,
As most abated captives to some nation
That won you without blows! Despising
For you the city, thus I turn my back.
There is a world elsewhere.
evidence.prefix: t shall be so, it shall be so!

questions.question: Why does Coriolanus offer his service to his former enemy Aufidius?

options.text: He wants Aufidius to help him distribute grain in Rome.
He hopes to replace Volumnia as a Roman diplomat.
He wants revenge on the Romans who banished him.
He has been sent to negotiate a Roman marriage alliance.

questions.explanation: Coriolanus offers to fight his own country so that his personal wrong can serve the Volscians.

evidence.exact:
CORIOLANUS.
My name is Caius Martius, who hath done
To thee particularly and to all the Volsces
Great hurt and mischief; thereto witness may
My surname Coriolanus. The painful service,
The extreme dangers, and the drops of blood
Shed for my thankless country are requited
But with that surname, a good memory
And witness of the malice and displeasure
Which thou shouldst bear me. Only that name remains.
The cruelty and envy of the people,
Permitted by our dastard nobles, who
Have all forsook me, hath devoured the rest,
And suffered me by th’ voice of slaves to be
Whooped out of Rome. Now this extremity
Hath brought me to thy hearth, not out of hope—
Mistake me not—to save my life; for if
I had feared death, of all the men i’ th’ world
I would have ’voided thee, but in mere spite,
To be full quit of those my banishers,
Stand I before thee here. Then if thou hast
A heart of wreak in thee, that wilt revenge
Thine own particular wrongs and stop those maims
Of shame seen through thy country, speed thee straight
And make my misery serve thy turn. So use it
That my revengeful services may prove
As benefits to thee, for I will fight
Against my cankered country with the spleen
Of all the under fiends. But if so be
Thou dar’st not this, and that to prove more fortunes
Thou ’rt tired, then, in a word, I also am
Longer to live most weary, and present
My throat to thee and to thy ancient malice,
Which not to cut would show thee but a fool,
Since I have ever followed thee with hate,
Drawn tuns of blood out of thy country’s breast,
And cannot live but to thy shame, unless
It be to do thee service.
evidence.prefix:
US.
I know thee not. Thy name?

questions.question: How does Coriolanus respond to Menenius's appeal to spare Rome?

options.text: He immediately dismisses the Volscian army.
He returns to Rome and asks to become consul again.
He allows Menenius to command the attack in his place.
He rejects the appeal despite their former friendship.

questions.explanation: Coriolanus tells Menenius that his ears are closed to Rome's petitions and refuses further speech.

evidence.exact:
CORIOLANUS.
Wife, mother, child, I know not. My affairs
Are servanted to others. Though I owe
My revenge properly, my remission lies
In Volscian breasts. That we have been familiar,
Ingrate forgetfulness shall poison rather
Than pity note how much. Therefore begone.
Mine ears against your suits are stronger than
Your gates against my force. Yet, for I loved thee,
Take this along; I writ it for thy sake,

questions.question: What effect does Volumnia's appeal have on Coriolanus?

options.text: He agrees to arrange peace rather than destroy Rome.
He orders her to lead the Volscian assault herself.
He abandons Aufidius and crowns himself king of Rome.
He refuses to speak with his wife or child again.

questions.explanation: Moved by his mother, Coriolanus acknowledges Rome's victory and undertakes to frame a peace.

evidence.exact:
CORIOLANUS.
O mother, mother!
What have you done? Behold, the heavens do ope,
The gods look down, and this unnatural scene
They laugh at. O my mother, mother, O!
You have won a happy victory to Rome,
But, for your son—believe it, O, believe it!—
Most dangerously you have with him prevailed,
If not most mortal to him. But let it come.—
Aufidius, though I cannot make true wars,
I’ll frame convenient peace. Now, good Aufidius,
Were you in my stead, would you have heard
A mother less? Or granted less, Aufidius?
evidence.prefix: olds her by the hand, silent.]

questions.question: What charge does Aufidius use against Coriolanus after the campaign?

options.text: They discover that he has ordered Volumnia's execution.
They accuse him of surrendering their victory by making peace.
They learn that he secretly gave Rome all their grain.
They blame him for refusing to leave the Roman Senate.

questions.explanation: Aufidius treats Coriolanus's mercy toward Rome as betrayal, and his conspirators kill him.

evidence.exact:
AUFIDIUS.
Ay, Martius, Caius Martius. Dost thou think
I’ll grace thee with that robbery, thy stol’n name
Coriolanus, in Corioles?
You lords and heads o’ th’ state, perfidiously
He has betrayed your business and given up
For certain drops of salt your city Rome—
I say your city—to his wife and mother,
Breaking his oath and resolution like
A twist of rotten silk, never admitting
Counsel o’ th’ war, but at his nurse’s tears
He whined and roared away your victory,
That pages blushed at him and men of heart
Looked wond’ring each at other.
[Draw the Conspirators, and kills Martius, who falls. Aufidius stands on him.]
